text:
The concept starts with the fact that the physical stimulus of the amniotic fluid plays a major role in lung
growth. This was a USMLE question: What is the stimulus for the growth of the lung in embryonic life? It
is the amniotic fluid. Without the amniotic fluid, it cannot grow.

Why? Because the baby is not breathing in embryonic life. There is no breathing, but the lung is still
growing. It is physical growth because the amniotic fluid goes through the canalicular stage and expands
it like a balloon. A balloon can only be expanded if you put air or fluid inside.

The lungs are half-filled with fluid derived from the amniotic cavity. When a baby is born, a suction pump
is used to take the fluid out of the lung for the first time. Then the baby cries, and the lung expands for the
first time. The lung can expand more over time, but initially, it is in proper shape because of this physical
growth.

If I ask you, 99.9% of lung growth depends on the amniotic fluid. Therefore, oligohydramnios (which is
associated with kidney disease) will seriously affect the growth of the lung. Remember that.





                                                                                                                   3

The respiratory organs begin to form during the fourth week. All organs are formed from the third week to
the eighth week, which is the critical period of organogenesis. The third week is for the cardiovascular
system because the heart is the first organ to become functional. The other organs, whether it is limb
development, the GI tract, the lung, or the endocrine system, start from the fourth week.

Initially, the starting point is a diverticulum. This is endoderm. It goes toward the esophagus, and one
goes to the trachea. It is connected because the baby is swallowing, and the fluid needs to go to both the
lung and the esophagus. Later, there is dissociation between the lung and the esophagus.

This connection is needed so that when the baby swallows amniotic fluid in embryonic life, it goes to the
lung and allows the lung to expand. Sometimes, a baby is born with this connection still intact, creating a
problem where you have to separate it very quickly. Otherwise, the baby will choke when drinking milk.
This is called a tracheoesophageal fistula.

(Dr. goes to Slide 6)





                                                                                                                   4

This diagram contains essential information. You have seen it earlier, and the concept is very important
because many questions on the USMLE and NBME were related to it. This slide is basically a section
from either the GI, the abdomen, or the thorax. The architecture is the same in the thorax and abdomen.

Let me orient you. We have the neural tube (spinal cord at the back), neural crest cells (migratory cells),
and the skin. These all come from the ectoderm. This photograph is after the lateral folding has taken
place.

Then you have the mesoderm: paraxial mesoderm, intermediate mesoderm, and lateral mesoderm. The
lateral mesoderm has two parts. One is the splanchnic mesoderm, supplied by the autonomic nervous
system. One is the somatic mesoderm, supplied by the somatic nerve. There is a space between them
called the intraembryonic coelom. This space forms because of folding and tube formation.

The endoderm forms a tube. In the GI system, it is the intestine. In the respiratory system, it is the lung or
the trachea. The lung, trachea, and bronchus are tubular structures. They all come from the endoderm.

Visualize the splanchnic mesoderm as the smooth muscle around the bronchus and trachea, supplied by
the autonomic nervous system. After that, you have the somatic muscle or somatic mesoderm, supplied
by the intercostal nerve or the phrenic nerve.

If I touch my chest, I am touching the skin. After that, I touch the intercostal muscle. If I go down, it's the
parietal pleura. The skin is from the ectoderm. The intercostal muscle and parietal pleura are from the
somatic mesoderm. All of them are supplied by the somatic nerve (intercostal or phrenic nerve). The
mediastinal area of the pleura is supplied by the phrenic nerve.


                                                                                                                   5

If you go deep down, there is the visceral pleura, then the bronchus, trachea, or lung (endoderm). There
is a space between the parietal pleura and visceral pleura called the pleural cavity. The splanchnic
mesoderm forms the visceral pleura, supplied by the autonomic nerve.

So, the layers are: skin (ectoderm), somatic mesoderm (intercostal muscle and parietal pleura), a space
(pleural cavity), splanchnic mesoderm (visceral pleura), and endoderm (the lung/trachea/bronchus tube).
This architecture is the same for the GI system and the thorax.

(Dr. goes to Slide 10)

Lung development depends on amniotic fluid. The tube has to expand, and this is not possible unless
there is fluid inside. You cannot expand a balloon without putting fluid or air inside. In embryonic life, the
embryo does not breathe, so the amniotic fluid goes inside the tube to expand it. This is physical growth.
After birth, the lung expands because of breathing, but in embryonic life, it is the amniotic fluid.

When does the expansion become impossible? When there is kidney disease, resulting in
oligohydramnios. Less urine means less amniotic fluid, which means less lung development.

Initially, the lung develops from the endoderm. It is a tube, but it starts as a solid structure that looks like a
gland. We call this the pseudoglandular stage. It was not a gland, but it looks like one. Then there is an
opening called the canalicular stage, where fluid can go inside and expand it. Then it becomes the
terminal sac stage, a critical period where surfactant is produced. Surfactant is needed for lung
expansion. Without it, survival is impossible. Finally, there is the alveolar stage.

There are four stages: pseudoglandular, canalicular, terminal sac, and alveolar. If a baby is delivered
prematurely in the pseudoglandular stage, the lung will not be developed and the baby will die. If
delivered in the canalicular stage, the baby will still die because there is no surfactant. The terminal sac
stage is the critical period. If a baby is born here and put in an incubator, the baby can survive. The
alveolar stage is the final stage where the baby should survive.

(Dr. goes to Slide 3)

If there is a muscle over here, that is the smooth muscle, coming from the splanchnic mesoderm.

(Dr. goes to Page 6 )





                                                                                                                   6

In the next photograph, if this is the trachea, it is surrounded by a red color. This is the splanchnic
mesoderm, forming smooth muscle. It is supplied by the autonomic nerve.

If it is surrounded by a muscle, it is coming from the splanchnic mesoderm. Which nerve supplies it? The
autonomic nervous system. Therefore, any muscle here is a smooth muscle. Now you understand, for
example, the bronchus: it has the endoderm, and the muscle and cartilage all come from the splanchnic
mesoderm. It is supplied by the autonomic nervous system.





                                                                                                                   7

The respiratory bud starts with the laryngotracheal diverticulum during the fourth week. Think about the
connection between the trachea and esophagus. Why does it need a connection? It is needed for lung
development. Lung development is physical and driven by amniotic fluid, which goes into both the
esophagus and the trachea to start with. That is why the connection is needed.

Should the connection be permanent? No, it dissociates after some time. If the connection persists, it is
an acute emergency situation that has to be surgically separated.





                                                                                                                   8

Look carefully at this diagram. You can see the connection, and then you see the dissociation where
there is no connection. This connection is needed because the baby is swallowing amniotic fluid, and the
fluid needs to go to both the esophagus and the lung.

When exactly does this happen? It all occurs within eight weeks; the dissociation happens within eight
weeks. The connection is called the tracheoesophageal septum or the diverticulum. It dissociates after
some time, and the esophagus and trachea remain independent structures.

In this diagram, you see the diverticulum. Diverticulum means two parts: one is going towards the
respiratory system, and one is going to the esophagus. Both are endoderm in origin. I am talking strictly
about the tube. It was connected initially, then it dissociates. That is what this photograph is all about.





                                                                                                                   9

Lung growth, branching of the lobes, and formation of the lung are just physical growth driven by the
formation of amniotic fluid going inside the canal. You do not need to read the text for this.

The key concept is the layers. If I put the skin here (ectoderm), then the intercostal muscle here (somatic
mesoderm), and then the parietal pleura (somatic mesoderm). Then there is a space called the pleural
cavity. After the space, you have the visceral pleura (splanchnic mesoderm) supplied by the autonomic
nervous system, and finally, the endoderm.

So, to review: the skin, intercostal muscle, and parietal pleura are supplied by the somatic nerve. Then
comes the pleural space, followed by the splanchnic mesoderm (visceral pleura), and then the endoderm.
If there is a muscle here, that is the smooth muscle coming from the splanchnic mesoderm.





                                                                                                                  10

Let's do this one. This is the lung. You can see it looks like a tube. It is the endoderm, the yellow color. It
is attached to a deep reddish color, not the pink, and that is the visceral pleura. The visceral pleura
comes from the splanchnic mesoderm and is supplied by the autonomic nervous system.

Then you have the pink color, which is the lateral mesoderm. This is the somatic one. The somatic
mesoderm forms the parietal pleura. So, you have the parietal pleura, the visceral pleura, and the
endoderm.

(Dr. goes to page 5.)





                                                                                                                  11

The growth finally reaches the pneumocyte type 1 and type 2, which is the final endpoint of lung
development. The lung becomes functional because of surfactant, which happens around 28 weeks (7
months). Type 2 pneumocytes produce surfactant, a phospholipid that enhances breathing and
expansion. Type 1 pneumocytes are squamous cells responsible for diffusion.

After birth, when the baby inhales, the lung can expand because of the surfactant, and this is possible
starting around 28 weeks. This is more detailed histology, but you can understand it from these
principles.





                                                                                                                  12

Now, this is the same structure as it bends.





                                                                                                                  14

You can see the bending is happening. The outside will be somatic, and the inside will be splanchnic.





                                                                                                                  15

You can see the splanchnic mesoderm, and next to it is the endoderm, the yellow color. You can tell what
this one is. These two are clear because it is written as the bronchial buds, but what is this one? It is the
esophagus. The yellow color represents the esophagus. So you have one esophagus and two bronchial
buds.





                                                                                                                  16

It will continue growing. You can see more growth occurring. The yellow color is the esophagus, and the
two lung buds are growing. The bronchial buds become the lung buds, and it starts to look like a lung.

Here is the interesting part. This is the chest because you can see the two heart tubes. This means it is in
the thorax. How are the different layers arranged here? This is the skin. Then the somatic mesoderm,
which includes the intercostal muscle and the parietal pleura. Then the pleural space. Then the
splanchnic mesoderm, which is the visceral pleura. And finally, the endoderm.

This photograph tells you a thousand words, and you should appreciate the concept rather than just
memorizing it. Somatic versus visceral: somatic means parietal pleura, and visceral means visceral
pleura or the splanchnic pleura. You can see the lung expanding, and there is still a space there. The
pleural cavity is still there, which is continuous with the intraembryonic coelom. The heart is joined there.





                                                                                                                  18

You can see the lung expanding, and there is still a space there. The pleural cavity is still present, which
is continuous with the intraembryonic coelom. The heart is joined over there.





                                                                                                                  19

You can see the junction now. The lung is over here. Again, this is the parietal pleura, this is the visceral
pleura, and there is the endoderm, which is the esophagus.

In this picture, the canalicular stage is already present, so the lung is expanding now.





                                                                                                                  20

Now for lung development. The initial period, from 6 to 16 weeks, is called the pseudoglandular stage. It
is a solid structure. A little bit of canalicular formation is there already, but the real canalicular stage is
from 16 to 26 weeks when the lung actually grows.

(Dr. goes to slide 19.)

The terminal sac stage is from 26 weeks to birth. It is an important stage for fetal viability because of
adequate surfactant production. In exams, they might ask why a baby born at 22 weeks dies. The baby
will die because, even in an incubator, the lung cannot expand without surfactant. In the terminal sac
stage, the baby can survive because surfactant is present.

Next is the alveolar stage, from 32 weeks to 8 years. The lung expands more due to air and surfactant,
and it continuously grows.

Remember these four stages:

1. Pseudoglandular stage: Solid stage.

2. Canalicular stage: Canals form where fluid can go inside.

3. Terminal sac stage: The most important part because viability is determined here. If a baby is born
   before 26 weeks, survival is unlikely because there is no surfactant. Surfactant is necessary and
   appears at 26 weeks. Modern technology might push survival to 25 weeks, but 22 or 23 weeks is
   impossible. Another reason is that the respiratory center in the brain is not developed yet. At 26
   weeks, the baby is likely to survive because of type 2 pneumocytes and surfactant.

4. Alveolar stage: This is simple; the lung will continuously grow.



                                                                                                                  21

Now, clinical embryology: oligohydramnios and lung development. Note that fluid in the lung during
embryonic life is an important stimulus for lung development. Physical growth is the most important factor
because the baby is not breathing in embryonic life. Lung development is directly proportional to the
swallowing reflex, as the amniotic fluid goes inside the canalicular stage to the lung and expands it.

Therefore, in oligohydramnios (which is associated with kidney disease), the lung cannot grow. Lung
development is retarded, meaning there is less development.

Lung development is also retarded in another situation that we will discuss in the next class. This
PowerPoint has two portions: the lung and the diaphragm. Next class, we will talk about the diaphragm
and congenital diaphragmatic hernia, where intestinal organs go into the thorax. The lung needs space
within the intraembryonic coelom. If that space is occluded by organs from the intestine, the lung will be
retarded.

So, lung development can be retarded in two situations: oligohydramnios, and a diaphragmatic hernia
where abdominal contents go into the thorax and the lung cannot grow. I will discuss the second one in
more detail next class.





                                                                                                                  22

Now, look at this situation carefully. The baby is born with the connection intact. You can see the
connection going to the esophagus and to the lung. This is called a tracheoesophageal fistula. Normally,
in this condition, the esophagus also does not grow properly; it is truncated.

When a baby is born with a tracheoesophageal fistula, they will experience a choking sensation when
drinking milk because the fluid is going to the lungs. This requires immediate surgery. If a baby is choking
after birth while drinking milk, you should think of a tracheoesophageal fistula. Most of the time,
esophageal atresia is also present.

In this scenario, what would the volume of the amniotic fluid be while the baby was in the uterus? It would
be increased, resulting in polyhydramnios. Why? Because the fluid is not going to the esophagus
properly. The baby is swallowing the fluid, but half of it is going to the lung and half of it is going out,
causing the fluid in the amniotic cavity to increase.

So, with a tracheoesophageal fistula, there will be polyhydramnios. As you can see, there are many types
of tracheoesophageal fistulas.





                                                                                                                  24

You only need to remember these two types. In the first type, esophageal atresia is not present. This is
the normal anatomy. Here, no connection is established. However, later on, you can see esophageal
atresia followed by a tracheoesophageal fistula. In other words, the fluid is going through the trachea.
That is why it is called a tracheoesophageal fistula. Remembering this one is good enough.

In this scenario, there is mostly esophageal atresia. So, esophageal atresia associated with a
tracheoesophageal fistula leads to polyhydramnios. Polyhydramnios is possible because of the
esophageal atresia and the fistula. A fistula means two openings. With a tracheoesophageal fistula, the
fluid accumulates, and there will be polyhydramnios. This is frequently asked in the exam.





                                                                                                                  25

Finally, we will discuss a medicolegal case. Sometimes, you will be asked to come to court to give an
explanation. Suppose you are a gynecologist, you deliver a baby, and the baby is dead. The mother
claims the baby was fine in her uterus and that the baby died because of something you did during
delivery. It becomes a legal case, and you have to prove that the baby was already dead before delivery.

To prove this in court, you can take the lung of the dead baby and put it in a bucket of water. If the lung
sinks, it means the baby never took a breath outside and was dead before. If the baby had taken a
breath, the lung would be full of air and would float. The lungs of a stillborn infant are firm and sink in
water because they contain fluid, not air.

If a mother claims the baby was alive in the uterus and died during delivery due to your mistake, you must
protect yourself by knowing the baby was dead before. How do you know? You put the baby's lung in a
bucket of water and it sinks. Why does it sink? Before birth, the lung is almost like a solid because it is not
participating in breathing. The lung is enlarged because of the amniotic fluid, but it has never been
functional. No air goes inside; the baby gets oxygen from the blood through the umbilical vein. The lung
does not expand or get any air in embryonic life, so it is like a solid brick and sinks in water.

If the baby is born normally, the first breath means air goes inside the lung for the first time. That means
the baby was alive. If the lung does not sink to the bottom of the container, it means the baby was alive
because the lung is floating. Thank you very much.
